sentences.text: If you dig a deep hole in your yard, you have a bunker.
But the first storm soaks the lawn and the rain pours straight into the hole.
Water fills the hole to the brim like a bathtub.
Wet soil weighs over 100 pounds per cubic foot, so the walls crack and cave in.
So you drain it, then pour a concrete floor and walls to hold the soil back.
Next you cap the box with a thick roof and pile three feet of soil on top.
Then you hang a steel door on the only way in, and the biggest ones weigh 25 tons.
Soil and concrete soak up the radiation, while the door and roof stop the blast wave.
Three feet of packed soil cuts gamma rays by a factor of about 1000.
But sealed in, the people keep breathing, and the air goes stale.
So you add a filter and a fan that pull fresh air down a pipe from outside.
But that pipe is a hole in the shield, and a blast wave would rush straight down it.
So you add a blast valve on the pipe that slams shut when the shock arrives.
And hiding underground for years is not what a bunker is really for.
Fallout fades fast, and after about 49 hours the radiation is down to around 1 percent.
Add a ceiling light, bunk beds, and the grass back on top.
Congratulations, you have built a nuclear bunker.
